lead: A real wing skin is stiffened by many stringers, so the direct stress varies continuously across the section and hand integration becomes long. Structural idealization replaces the section by a few booms that carry all the direct stress and thin panels that carry only shear. Each boom sits at a stringer position and is given an effective area that includes the skin working with it. The panels keep the real skin thickness. A hard integral becomes a short sum over booms. Shear-flow, shear-centre and torsion calculations for wing and fuselage boxes start this way.
prereq: You need 5.2 for the shear flow sum and Unit 4 for direct stress in bending.

sections.h3: Booms carry direct stress, panels carry shear

blocks.text: A wing box has skin, stringers, ribs and spars. Under bending, the stringers and the skin next to them carry almost all the direct stress. The thin skin between stringers carries very little direct stress but carries shear well.

The idealized section keeps this split. Each stringer plus its share of skin becomes one boom. A boom is a line area that carries only direct stress σ, in N/mm². The skin between booms becomes a panel of thickness t, in mm, that carries only shear flow q, in N/mm.

The boom has area B, in mm², and position (x, y) from a chosen origin. The panel has length b, in mm, and thickness t. The panel is treated as carrying a constant shear flow along its length. The whole section is then a ring of booms joined by panels.

This is also called the lumped-area method or stringer–skin idealization. It is used for wing boxes, fuselage frames and tail surfaces. The figure shows the chain from a real section to panel shear flows.

blocks.where: B is the effective boom area in mm²; A<sub>stringer</sub> is the stringer area in mm²; t is the skin thickness in mm; b is the sum of the two full skin widths working with the boom, b = b₁ + b₂, in mm; σ<sub>skin</sub> is the direct stress in the skin and σ<sub>boom</sub> the direct stress in the stringer, both in N/mm².

blocks.text: t·b is the skin area working with the boom; the factor 1/6 comes from the parabolic stress build-up in the skin. The term (2 + σ<sub>skin</sub>/σ<sub>boom</sub>) accounts for the skin on both sides of the stringer and for the skin working at a different stress from the stringer. When both work at the same stress the bracket is 3, so B = A<sub>stringer</sub> + t·b/2. For equal panels at pitch p, b = 2p, so B = A<sub>stringer</sub> + t·p.

A corner boom is shared by two panels. Use b = b₁ + b₂, so the skin contribution is (t/6)(b₁ + b₂)(2 + σ<sub>skin</sub>/σ<sub>boom</sub>). A boom on a straight run with skin on both sides uses b = b₁ + b₂, which is twice the pitch when the panels are equal.

items: Mark every stringer position on the section.
Give each boom b = b₁ + b₂: the two full skin widths working with it. For equal panels at pitch p, b = 2p.
Choose the stress ratio. For a first check take σ<sub>skin</sub>/σ<sub>boom</sub> = 1.
Compute B for every boom. For a corner boom use b₁ + b₂.
Replace the real section by these booms and the skin panels.

sections.h3: Section properties and panel shear flow

blocks.where: I<sub>xx</sub> is the second moment of area about the horizontal centroidal axis in mm⁴; B is a boom area in mm²; y is the boom height from that axis in mm. The sum runs over all booms.
σ is the direct stress in a boom in N/mm²; M is the bending moment in N·mm; y is the boom height from the neutral axis in mm; I<sub>xx</sub> is in mm⁴.

blocks.text: For a vertical shear force S, in N, cut the section at a panel and sum the boom terms from the cut to the point considered:

blocks.where: q is the shear flow in N/mm in the panel at the cut-off point; S is the vertical shear force in N; I<sub>xx</sub> is in mm⁴; the sum is over the booms cut off between the free edge and that point.

blocks.text: The sum is over booms only, not over the panel. The panel thickness sets the shear stress, τ = q/t, but not q itself. In a closed box, add the constant q₀ from 5.3 so the twist is correct. In a symmetric box under vertical shear, q₀ is zero.

figure.caption: The real stringer–skin section becomes four corner booms of area 750 mm² joined by 2 mm panels. The vertical shear of 15 kN gives 37.5 N/mm in each web panel and zero in the top and bottom panels.

examples.question: A rectangular wing box is 400 mm wide and 200 mm deep. It has four corner booms, each with stringer area 150 mm², and a skin 2 mm thick. Take σ<sub>skin</sub>/σ<sub>boom</sub> = 1. Find the effective boom areas, I<sub>xx</sub>, and the panel shear flows for a vertical shear force S = 15 kN.
steps: Each corner boom is shared by a 400 mm flange panel and a 200 mm web panel. So b₁ = 400 mm and b₂ = 200 mm.
Effective boom area B = A<sub>stringer</sub> + 600 = 150 + 600 = 750 mm².
The four booms sit at y = +100 mm and y = −100 mm from the horizontal centroidal axis. I<sub>xx</sub> = Σ B·y² = 4 × 750 × (100)² = 30,000,000 mm⁴ = 3.0 × 10⁷ mm⁴.
Cut the top panel at its midpoint. Moving left to the top-left boom, the boom cut off has y = +100 mm. q = −(S/I<sub>xx</sub>)B·y = −(15000/30000000)(750)(100) = −37.5 N/mm.

The left web panel carries this q = −37.5 N/mm down to the bottom-left boom. That boom has y = −100 mm; its contribution (15000/30000000)(750)(100) = +37.5 N/mm cancels the first, so q after it is zero.
Moving along the bottom panel gives q = 0, then the bottom-right boom adds +37.5 N/mm to the right web. The right web carries +37.5 N/mm. The top panel closes the loop at q = 0.

The minus and plus signs appear because the loop is traced downwards on the left web and upwards on the right web. Both webs carry shear in the same direction, opposing the applied 15 kN, and 2 × 37.5 N/mm × 200 mm = 15 kN checks the balance.
Magnitudes: each web panel carries 37.5 N/mm; the top and bottom panels carry zero.
examples.answer: Each effective boom area is 750 mm², I<sub>xx</sub> = 3.0 × 10⁷ mm⁴, and the vertical shear of 15 kN gives 37.5 N/mm in each web panel and zero in the top and bottom panels.
examples.check:
A = 150
t = 2
b1 = 400
b2 = 200
ratio = 1
B = A + (t*(b1+b2)/6)*(2+ratio)
Ixx = 4*B*100**2
S = 15000
q = S*B*100/Ixx
print(B)
print(Ixx)
print(q)

traps: Counting the skin twice: the effective skin width belongs to the boom, but the panel still exists and still carries shear. Do not delete the panel.
Using one panel width for a corner boom shared by two panels. Use b₁ + b₂ for the two panels meeting at the corner.
Forgetting that the sum ΣB·y in the shear-flow formula runs over booms only. Adding panel areas to the sum gives a wrong q.
Mixing units: S in N, y in mm and I in mm⁴ give q in N/mm. Using S in kN gives a q that is 1000 times too small.
In a closed box, stopping at the basic q without adding q₀. The basic q alone does not satisfy zero twist.

quiz.q: State the two things a boom and a panel each carry in an idealized section.
quiz.a: A boom carries only direct stress (axial stress). A panel carries only shear flow.

quiz.q: Why is the effective boom area larger than the stringer area?
quiz.a: Because the skin next to the stringer carries direct stress too. Its share, over the pitch b, is added to the stringer area so the boom represents both.

quiz.q: A stringer of area 120 mm² has 1.5 mm skin panels 80 mm wide on each side (pitch 80 mm). Take σ<sub>skin</sub>/σ<sub>boom</sub> = 1. Find B.
quiz.a: b = b₁ + b₂ = 160 mm; B = 120 + (1.5 × 160/6)(2 + 1) = 120 + 40 × 3 = 240 mm². If the stringer had skin on one side only over 80 mm, B would be 180 mm²; the question must say so.

quiz.q: Four booms of area 500 mm² sit at y = ±150 mm. Find I<sub>xx</sub>.
In a symmetric four-boom box under vertical shear, why are the top and bottom panel shear flows zero?
quiz.a: In a box symmetric about the vertical centre line, the shear flow at the mid-point of the top flange must be zero, because the flows arriving from the two mirror-image halves would have to be equal and opposite at the same cut. Starting from that zero-flow cut, no boom lies between the cut and the top corner, so the whole top panel carries zero flow, and the bottom panel likewise by symmetry. The two webs each carry a flow q = S/(2h), where S is the shear force and h the depth, so the vertical shear splits equally between them; both flows act in the same direction, opposing S.

quiz.q: A student doubles the skin thickness and also doubles every panel width in the idealized model. What happens to B and to the panel shear flows?
quiz.a: B rises because the skin contribution rises. If the boom positions stay the same and every boom area grows by the same factor k, then I<sub>xx</sub> grows by k and the product B·y grows by k, so q = (S/I<sub>xx</sub>)B·y is unchanged. If the wider panels also make the box twice as deep, each web carries a flow q = S/(2h), which halves for the same S. The thicker panels then carry the flow at half the shear stress, τ = q/t.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production stress offices use idealized sections with hundreds of booms and panels, solved by matrix methods. The same lumped-area idea feeds finite-element shell models, where Stringer elements and shear panels appear explicitly. Search for "boom idealization", "shear panel idealization" and "idealized wing box shear flow" to go further. Tapered and combined open-closed cases follow in 5.7 and 5.8.
